Question: What is the best way to make chicken breasts juicy and tender when baking in oven?
Answer: A couple of things help with preventing dry boneless and skinless chicken breasts. A breading helps keep moisture in and it’s quite important not to overcook the chicken. The internal temperature should be 165 F when removed from the oven. The breasts should then rest for a few minutes. I like to use breast cutlets, split boneless/skinless breasts myself, or pound chicken breasts to a thin and uniform thickness under plastic wrap. Preheat the oven to 425F. Place the breasts on an oiled baking sheet, lined or unlined and dry them with paper towels. Sprinkle the chicken on both sides with salt and pepper, and brush them on the top side with an even layer of sour cream. You can also use mayonnaise or an egg wash instead of the cream. Mix 1 part by volume of Panko bread crumbs with 3/4 parts grated parmesan cheese and a large drizzle of olive oil or melted butter. Chopped herbs like parsely, a little lemon zest, a little more salt and pepper, or grated garlic can also be added to the Panko mix if you like. Mix well and pack the top of the breasts with the Panko mixture. It’s not really necessary to coat both sides of the chicken, but you can, of course. For 4 cutlets, coated on one side, I use 1/2 cup of Panko and 1/3 cup of grated cheese. Spray the breaded tops lightly with an oil spray and bake these on the center oven rack for 15 to 20 minutes, removing when the internal temperature is 165 F. Rest for 5 to 10 minutes and serve. Photo from Spend with Pennies.

If budgeting, try chicken or thicker pork chops. Sides? - I love baked beans (with ground beef sometimes), potato salad, baked potato, or a potato casserole, and grilled jalapeño poppers. - Corn on the cob is great grilled naked (the corn), directly on the grill until speckled like a Dalmatian). - Asparagus, or slices of eggplant with tomato sauce and mozzarella. Dessert? - Grilled fresh peach halves with ice cream are tasty and impressive. - Most folks love homemade ice cream.

Question: What gives banana pudding its creamy texture? Is there a secret ingredient used in its preparation?
Answer: I make banana pudding at the McCune house periodically and I have no secrets. In fact, I’m well known for blurting out things that would be better kept in my mouth. A typical American banana pudding is a vanilla custard with sliced bananas, vanilla wafers and is often served with whipped cream or with a baked meringue topping. The vast majority of these puddings are made with gelatin mixes, but I don’t do that, since the custard is stupidly simple and quick to make from scratch. It’s also much better tasting and is smooth. To enhance the banana flavor, I include a well-mashed banana in the custard as it cooks, but that’s not necessary and tends to be slightly less smooth than a vanilla custard. Whether slicing or mashing, use bananas that are just ripe, easily sliced and won’t darken the pudding. If you incorporate the bananas just after slicing, they don’t have time to discolor. If the banana slices are exposed, brushing with a little lemon juice helps maintain color.

Question: Do you have any simple soup recipes? Can you list all of their ingredients and procedures?
Answer: I can post recipes (and will if you need them) but the key to most broth-based soups is excellent stock. Ask any Jewish, Asian or any grandmother famous for her chicken soup and she will answer, “bones.” I’ve heard them say that; yes I have. If you’ve ever slurped noodles from a bowl of Vietnamese Pho Bo or Pho Ga, you’ll catch yourself saying, “Ohooo, that’s soooo good.” Pho is usually the best broth in town and worth seeking out. But, I made a pot of chicken noodle soup this week that brought out the same moans as I sipped bowls and bowls of it. Good stock is made with fresh bones, meat with connective tissue, and vegetables and is cooked until the gelatin enriches the broth. When chilled, it should gel. You can make that yourself, talk Granny into giving you a quart or two, pay extra to purchase really good stock or buy stock concentrates. They run a little less than a dollar per small packet and are worth the price. I make reasonable stock in my Instant Pot pressure cooker in a couple of hours or on the stove top for much longer, using chicken bones or left over rotisserie chickens after the meat has been picked. Onions, celery, carrots and other vegetable trimmings go into the pot too, but hold the salt. Another key to an excellent soup is the perfect amount of salt which can only be intentionally obtained at the end of cooking the soup. If you’ve ever purchased Hello Fresh or other recipe-and-food delivery service, you’ve probably used the small packets of concentrated stock (vegetable, chicken, beef). Check online or at your favorite store for these, but they really bring soups and dishes to life. Avoid the store brand boxes of broth (unless you use them to make homemade stock), and buy the boxed unsalted stock for emergency use, but lean toward making your own stock or going with concentrates.

Question: What are canned biscuits?
Answer: Canned biscuits are containers of dough for American-style biscuits, similar to scones. The dough is divided into disks, packed into a cardboard tube with seams, and covered with a paper that can be easily peeled away from the cardboard tube. Once the paper cover is peeled away, the tube can be pressed on its spiral seam with the edge of a spoon or the tube can be “whacked” or”Whopped” on the edge of a counter. When the seal is broken, the tube famously “pops,” loudly and the cardboard can be peeled away, exposing the dough and individual sections. These are baked and the chemical leavening will raise the biscuits as they cook. I was blessed once in 1973 to see Jerry Clower, the comedian from Yazoo City, Mississippi before I ever heard of him and he is famous for having opinions about canned biscuits. His Momma made hog-lard biscuits in a wooden bowl that he called “cat-head” biscuits because they were that big. He further moaned about women in Yazoo City who would “whop” those refrigerated biscuit tubes on their countertop edges until it sounded like a young war breaking out on Slazey Street. Jerry said “I want to get the news out! I don’t eat them kind of biscuits! I ain’t that hen-pecked!”

I spooned the mixture into an oiled, heated, cast iron skillet and spread into patty shapes. The patties (also called fritters) were done in no time, were lower in carbs, and offered fiber and other good nutrients. Question: Why aren’t there any Apple or grape flavors of ice cream in ice cream parlors?
Answer: Apples are featured in ice creams, but not in overwhelming numbers, but grapes get a pass and for good reasons. In the ‘60s, Dutch Apple ice cream was a favorite flavor in Cabell’s ice cream for my family. Cabell’s was a Texas company that had a dairy line and over 60 convenience stores. Cabell’s was purchased by Southland Corp. in 1959 which owned 7-Eleven stores. As a kid in Texas, I worked at several Cabell’s Minit Markets and the ice cream line was excellent. Today, the Dutch Apple flavor can still be enjoyed but is rare, however, other apple flavored ice creams can be found such as apple pie, caramel apple, and apple swirl flavors. Now grapes have so much water, that they become little chunks of ice when frozen and just don’t lend themselves to making good ice cream (see Note). According to mashed.com, there's an urban legend that Ben Cohen (the front half of Ben & Jerry's) once made a batch of grape ice cream that killed Jerry's sister's dog, and swore off all further attempts. I don’t believe that, but I haven’t seen a grape flavored ice cream, either. NOTE: As pointed out in the comments, grapes have no more water than apples and other fruits found in ice cream). Also in comments, grape ice cream is made in Japan and other places.

Question: What has been your most memorable experience, for good or for bad, with another passenger on an airline flight?
Answer: I think it was in the ‘80s when I talked to a fellow passenger on a long flight. I was fumbling to open a package of peanuts or other snack and he mentioned he worked for one of the last companies to manufacture cellophane which used to dominate clear plastic packaging. What I remembered about cellophane was the noise it generated when crumpled. The plastic of the ’80s was often coated with vaporized metals such as aluminum and were virtually silent when crinkled. He explained that plastic wrappers such as the one I was trying to open were under scrutiny because they were not biodegradable like cellophane. I was interested as much of my engineering work was environmental in nature. He mentioned that some companies were attaching starch molecules to their plastic product to allow them to break apart as the starch decomposed and reduce their impact on the environment. He was looking forward to an increase in use of cellophane for environmental reasons. His, he said, was one of only three producers of cellophane. I thought at the time, “I should invest in cellophane companies,” but I never acted on that. Today, most clear packages and many snack packages I see rattle when scrunched. I think I missed the boat on a great investment. I have read that the replacement polyester plastics of the ’80s and ’90s have moved over to allow cellophane to resurge in usage. Darn, I missed it.

Question: What is the best diploma to pursue between plant engineering and production engineering?
Answer: You’ll need an engineering degree, not just a diploma and the two terms you use for types of engineering have various meanings for different industries. I am a retired chemical engineer who worked in 2 types of industries and in various capacities doing both chemical and environmental work. Most of that work was technical support but some could be called production engineering in the chemical and aluminum industries. A technical position is what I call plant engineering, and being in charge of producing a particular product or function could be production engineering. An engineering degree (mechanical, industrial, chemical, petroleum. electrical, etc.) usually opens an initial door in a company. It could be supervising a section of a facility (production engineering) or a technical support position (plant engineering). In my case, it was with a design team in the chemical industry. From the initial position you move according to your interests and abilities through the company based a good deal on your accomplishments, interests and relationships. You may move inside a company and its subsidiaries (as I did for 41 years) or outside to other companies. Just focus on the type of degree that interests you, learning what you can about the type of work that usually leads to, and seek a company that interests you in what they do and consider their reputation.

Question: Who usually cooks your favorite dish at home? What is the dish and who taught them how to make it?
Answer: My wife, The Warden, insists on cooking Thanksgiving dinner except for the turkey, dinner rolls, and giblet gravy. She’s a very good cook but doesn’t like to cook often. I, on the other hand, love to cook and I cook often. At Thanksgiving, my favorite dish is her cornbread dressing. She learned to cook dressing from her mother in their small Alabama town which is part of a quad city area. I first cook a large turkey and remove it from the roaster when it’s done. She starts by making two large cast iron skillets of cornbread. She sautés a large quantity of onions and celery in butter. She separates the turkey fat from its drippings, tosses the fat, and reserves the drippings. The cornbread is then finely crumbled into the roaster and mixed with the onion - celery mixture, a generous amount of sage, chopped boiled eggs, cream of chicken soup, evaporated milk, the drippings and additional broth as needed. She adds salt and pepper to taste and bakes until golden brown. The best part is tasting before it is cooked. I make giblet gravy for the dressing and it’s a chicken gravy with chopped giblets or, more often, diced dark turkey. I must have gravy on her dressing. I love this dressing hot or cold and I embarrass myself by how much I eat. I’ve enjoyed it for about 40 Thanksgivings and, God willing, more to come. It’s in the roaster in the center of the photo.

Question: Can you provide some recipes for a cajun jambalaya with sausage, chicken, shrimp, and crawfish?
Answer: Cajun jambalaya is brown while Creole is a red jambalaya because of tomatoes. In fact, the presence of tomatoes is a very common marker for Creole dishes. You’ve also listed four proteins with two being seafood. It’s a personal choice but I’d use either crawfish or shrimp, not both, but you do you. Question: What are the main differences between the Hamburg and Salisbury steak?
Answer: Hamburg Steak in the U.S. has changed so much that it is almost impossible to compare with a Salisbury Steak. But a Hamburg Steak in Germany or Japan is very similar to Salisbury steak. A Hamburg steak in Germany, Japan, and other countries where it is popular is a blend of ground beef or beef and pork, eggs, bread crumbs, and seasonings and a little milk. This is formed into a patty and pan-fried. It is served as a patty and not in a sandwich and usually is topped with a reduction pan sauce. It is often served with vegetables. A Hamburg steak in the U.S. in the late 19th Century was minced beef served raw or barely cooked. This changed in this country until it was became the hamburgers of today without fillers like breadcrumbs, eggs, and others. But this is a hamburger steak, not a true Hamburg steak. The Salisbury Steak was developed in the late 19th century by Dr. James H. Salisbury, an American who believed in a diet with lots of lean beef. It is essentially, a German or Japanese Hamburg steak with breadcrumbs, eggs, and milk. It differs from Hamburg steak some in the serving and topping. Salisbury steaks are cooked and removed from the pan, so that a brown gravy can be made in the pan. The patties are then returned to the pan and simmered in the gravy. Mushrooms can be included in the gravy and it is usually served over mashed potatoes or rice. Hamburg Steak is usually topped with a pan sauce and served with vegetables. Question: Who were the three American heroes who died at the Alamo?
Answer: You are asking about the three leaders represented below; however, ~189 volunteers, all considered heroes by many, died in the siege and battle of the ex-mission and fort called the Alamo. I’m no historian, but I was raised in Texas where we didn’t study Texas History in school, but had Alamo I and Alamo II instead. I also watched John Wayne’s 1960 movie, “The Alamo,” which doesn’t qualify me as an historian either. In 1836, the Alamo was occupied by Mexican troops who had years earlier seized the mission and taken the land for military purposes. Texas volunteers then overtook the garrison and were determined to hold it. Colonel James Bowie and Lieutenant Colonel William B. Travis commanded the troops in the Alamo. David Crockett. an ex-U.S. congressman from Tennessee arrived at the Alamo with a small group of men. This all occurred in the month of February, 1836, but the seige and battle for the Alamo lasted from February 23 through March 6. William “Buck” Travis was a lawyer from North Carolina who was a Lieutenant Colonel in the Texas military. He was celebrated as a hero by locals in Anahauc, Texas where the first shots of the Texas Revolution were fired. He was an extremely determined leader as he is rumored to have drawn the famous “line in the sand” for those to cross who were willing to die at the Alamo for defending it. Sharing leadership at the Alamo was James Bowie, a colonel in the Revolution and well known as a smuggler, slave trader and for his “Bowie” knife. He and Travis did not get along until the next leader arrived to still troubled waters. David Crockett, never known as Davy until a TV show was made about him, arrived with a few men, known as sharp shooters with long rifles, some from Tennessee. David failed in winning his third term in the US Congress and fell out with Andrew Jackson over the Indian Removal Act. As he left Washington he famously said “You can all go to Hell - I’m going to Texas.” And he and his buddies did. David was a cheerful fellow that encouraged others with tall tales and his fiddle. I doubt he killed a bear at age 3 as was advertised. The other leader of note was Antonio López de Santa Anna, who served as President of Mexican several times. Santa Anna had a “no prisoners” policy, a determination to retake the Alamo, and from 1800 to 6000 men marching to the Alamo. “His most serene Highness,” Santa Anna killed 189 men at the Alamo and moved on to kill 342 Texan prisoners at the Goliad Massacre a few weeks later. Whether David Crockett died in the Alamo or was captured along with 6 or 7 others and immediately killed in front of Santa Anna is debated and, I think, is inconsequential. Question: When measured in something like a measuring cup, does 10 teaspoons of ketchup cover the same amount of area as 10 teaspoons of water?
Answer: When first poured (or squeezed) out, a ketchup spill covers less surface area than the same volume of water does. However, if you shake the surface the ketchup has spilled upon, the ketchup will become less viscous (less thick, if you will) and will spread out much like water does. Ketchup is a non-Newtonian fluid that becomes less viscous when stress forces are applied. Water is a Newtonian fluid with a predictable viscosity based on temperature. Water molecules slip over each other while parts of ketchup (pulp, water, etc.) tend to pile up or stick to surfaces until force is applied. That's why I can invert a bottle of ketchup and most of the liquid stays in the bottle until I thump the bottom of the bottle and then it moves freely … for a while.

Question: What kind of plant can eat bugs?
Answer: They are called carnivorous plants and there are a bunch of types and species within the types. One type is triggered to trap bugs when they land on the plants. The most well known perhaps is the Venus Flytrap plant native to North and South Carolina, a few hours drive from where I live in Georgia. But, there are other plants like the bladderwort that are triggered into action when insects are detected. This one below … isn’t real - not even close. But, here are five real types of carnivorous plant families. Pitfall plants (not pitiful) attract insects or small vertebrates by a nectar and have sufaces (slippery or down-turned hairs) that discourage inspects from escaping. Many are called pitcher plants and some are quite attractive. Sticky plants operate like flypaper with solutions that are very sticky and trap insects. Secretions then digest the bugs. This is a sundew plant, with sticky mucilage on long glands to act as flypaper. Snapping plants are triggered to enclose insects when sensed. The Venus Fly Trap has been discussed above. Bladder plants are water plants that, when insects are detected on the surface, suck water in to entrain water fleas and other tiny insects into small, underwater cavities that enclose the bugs. Lobster plants are, like the lobster traps fishermen use, easy to enter, and difficult to exit. Spirally arranged hairs are used to trap the insects and move them downward to root-like digestive areas.

Question: What is happening to meat bones as they are being cooked for a stock?
Answer: What happens to bones simmering in water has a lot to do with collagen which are proteins in the structural portions of animal bodies. Collagen resides in the structural portions of an animal such as connective tissue, cartilage, bones, tendons, ligaments, and skin. So, bones are an important source of collagen. When collagen is hydrolyzed by cooking, it melts and forms gelatin. It is the amount of gelatin or hydrolyzed collagen that differentiates a broth from a stock. Cooking bones for a substantial amount of time melts collagen into gelatin, extracts and dissolves it the water, making stock. This adds a substantial amount of body and flavor to the water the bones are in which distinguishes it from broth. In my opinion, and in summary, water is okay to use in cooking, but broth is better, and rich stock is superior. Image Source: http://i.ytimg.com

Question: What is the recommended resting time for pizza dough before shaping and baking if you do not want to wait overnight?
Answer: This resting time is just a personal preference in regard to flavor. The normal steps with yeast doughs are mixing, kneading, bulk fermentation, shaping, proofing (fermenting again) and baking. The more time we spend letting the dough ferment until it doubles in volume (or just 150% more volume), the better the flavor. This extra time can be had by fermenting at room temperature with less yeast, pre-fermenting some of the dough before mixing all of the dough, or letting the dough rise in the fridge. If you are going to make the pizza in consecutive steps on the same day, I recommend using less yeast than your recipe calls for and letting the dough rise in a straight-sided clear container marked at the initial level of dough. When the dough has risen 1 1/2 to 2 times its initial volume, proceed with the steps. After shaping (dividing and stretching) the individual crusts, I will usually put the toppings on, cover with plastic wrap, and let the crusts rise for 20 minutes or so before baking. Question: Senior Citizens: What is the difference between a walking stick and a cane?

Walking canes don’t really go by many other names, while walking sticks are also called trekking sticks, hiking sticks or wading sticks (for the stream fishermen among us) and “sticks” is often replaced with “staffs,” or “poles.” Both canes and sticks come in a variety of materials, with wood and aluminum being popular and some are adjustable in height. Some are collapsable, readily popping back into full length thanks to an elastic center cord. My wading staff is like that and can be assembled with a flick of my wrist while wading in current on slippery rocks. Question: How do I freeze Roma tomatoes without peeling them?

To flash freeze, wash and dry ripe plum tomatoes place spaced apart on a parchment lined baking sheets. Place in the freezer for a couple of hours or longer to freeze. This assures the tomatoes don’t freeze in a large lump, but the shape of plum tomatoes especially with peels on, tend not to lump together much. While I have only blanched, quenched, slip-peeled and frozen tomatoes, there are many articles (often by homesteaders) online teaching that once thawed for a bit, the skins slip right off and can be further thawed, cut and cooked as you need. Some folks wash, dry, de-stem and quarter plum tomatoes with their skins on. Once drained on kitchen paper and flash frozen, these can be bagged without sticking together. Keep in mind that freezing changes the texture so that using in salads is not as likely as using in cooking.

Question: What are the differences between pickling and fermentation?
Answer: Both processes preserve food and produce a tart, tasty product and there is an abundance of confusion and overlap just for kicks. To simplify, let’s talk about cucumbers and not other veggies that are pickled or fermented. Pickling is defined as immersing something in an acidic solution like vinegar or a brine like salt water. We make quick pickles at home by salting cucumbers, rinsing, and then immersing them in a vinegar, water and sugar solution. These are refrigerated for short periods or frozen for enjoying months later. Fermentation is an old school process of allowing friendly bacteria called lactobacillus, to ferment something and produce lactic acid. These bacteria eat the natural sugars in the cucumbers to produce lactic acid which preserves vegetables or fruit in a similar fashion as pickling. Fermenting cucumbers starts with a brine and some cucumbers that is allowed over a few weeks at room temperature to produce an acidic solution by the action of our friendly neighborhood bacteria. At the McCune house, our roux is usually made dry (oil-less) by browning flour in a cast-iron skillet, stirring/whisking continuously. Question: Which of the gas laws is responsible for pressure cookers exploding, Boyle's law, Charles' law, or Gay-Lussac's law? I take Gay Lussac’s law.
Answer: I say none of the above. Saturated steam does not follow the laws for ideal gasses and Lussac’s law deals with mixtures of liquids and their partial pressures. A pressure cooker is filled with 1 liquid, water, so Lussac’s law becomes the vapor pressure of water. So, what does apply is the vapor pressure of water at different temperatures and, really, whether the pressure cooker can hold the pressures inside. The real question is about the design of the cooker and are there any failures in the safety features? When I put a cup or two of water into my pressure cooker, the system follows the vapor pressure of water. A steam table tells us that at atmospheric pressure, water and steam are in equilibrium at 212F. At 10 more pounds per square inch (psig) pressure, the temperature is 239F. At 15 psig, the temperature is approximately 250F. Keep those pressure cookers cleaned and maintained and they will be safe.

Question: What is the purpose of using white gravy with southern fried chicken? Can brown gravy be used instead?
Answer: In some parts of the South, it’s a thing going waaaay back, but I can’t tell you why. When I moved from Texas to Georgia 40 something years ago, I was surprised to find gravy, say, at breakfast bars that was essentially béchamel. There’s nothing wrong with béchamel, I love it, but béchamel is not what I’m used to seeing called gravy. In Georgia, It is called cream gravy, white gravy or milk gravy. In Texas, white gravies are common but they are not really white. The roux is usually cooked until it is a golden or tan color and whatever fat was used to cook the meat was likely used in the gravy. Both of these bring flavor into the gravy. In fact, the word gravy is usually defined as a sauce made with cooked meat or at least the fat from cooking the meat. As far as gravy for fried chicken, it is common, but gravy with chicken fried steak is much more common, at least in the parts of the Southern ridges I run. When I make chicken gravy, I use chicken broth instead of milk. For no good reason, I do like milk gravy on chicken fried steak, but, I put some color in the roux and may very well mix milk and chicken broth. I’ll finish by saying here in my small Georgia town, my favorite restaurant does offer brown or cream gravy with their chicken fried (or country fried) steak. The brown gravy option is with dark brown gravy and not gravy made with chicken broth. EDIT: I read a Washington Post article by Aaron Hutcherson on the history of milk gravy. In the Southern Appalachian mountains during the late 1800s, hearty breakfasts were necessary in the lumber industry and work life in general. Milk and flour were affordable and sausage was common when funds allowed meat or a hog was butchered. Question: Why does iron not rust other gases, not with oxygen?
Answer: Rust is iron(III) oxide with a few water molecules hanging around. Most oxidizing elements (oxygen, chlorine, fluorine, iodine gasses for example) will react with iron. Oxygen is just so prevalent in earth’s atmosphere, most metals are found in an oxidized (rusted, sort-of) state. Silicon dioxide or silica (as in quartz or sand) is a good example. Pure silicon doesn’t exist naturally and has to be prepared. The same is true for iron. If a ball of iron wool is heated and immersed in gaseous chlorine, it will “burn,” or oxidize to release heat and light, forming iron(III)chloride in the absence of oxygen. Question: Can bromine exist naturally?
Answer: Bromine, the element, is not abundant in nature, and is never found as a free element. It is present as salts and is found in sea water. Sodium bromide salt is a common form. It is recovered from brines in underground sources (in Arkansas and Michigan, I believe) and from the Dead Sea. I worked for a chemical plant in Arkansas for nine years where we pumped brine from underground formations, reacted the sodium bromide present with chlorine gas, which released the element bromine. The yields of okra, squash, cucumbers, carrots, peppers and tomatoes were poor. Herbs like oregano, sage, rosemary and parsley did well and are still growing a year later. This year, in those beds, I planted lettuces, collards, and onion starts and those all are doing pretty well. Tomatoes in that spot are still not doing well and neither are the peppers I planted. Across the yard is a spot that gets six or so hours of sunlight and tomatoes I planted in pots are thriving. So, do yourself a favor and take the recommendations for sunlight on the plant identification cards seriously.

Question: How does the thickness of aluminum foil affect its ability to retain heat when used for cooking or wrapping food?
Answer: Covering is more important for retaining heat than what is used. As long as the foil covering is compatible with the food and continuous, its thickness isn’t that important. In other words, in cooking, I don’t think heat loss (or gain) by conduction is as strong a factor as is trapping steam, radiation, and convection are. How the foil holds up is important and thickness plays a role, however, in cooking and in freezing foods. As a old engineer, I’ve forgotten most of my heat transfer stuff but I do remember sizing heating systems for tanks of all sizes. The vast majority of the heat loss was almost always from the surface. Any effective cover, even ping-pong balls floating on top, worked to keep heat in. With cooking, a cover reduces heat loss from evaporation primarily and pots heat up more quickly and covered baking items tend to steam-cook or braise. Foil also controls browning from radiated heat regardless of its thickness. With freezing, it’s all about sealing the food and keeping air out. Thickness is important here as thin foil tends to tear in the freezer. That would be “tearible.”

Question: Is there a cereal that a diabetic can eat without having sugar or starch in it?

Question: How do you handle p,v, t in case of pressure cookers (thermodynamics, ideal gas, gas, physics)?
Answer: I don’t consider this a case for ideal gas laws because the steam is saturated and in equilibrium with water in the pressure cooker. (See Notes below). The temperature and pressures behave along known paths for saturated steam and these are available in steam tables. Volumes don’t really matter as long as your pot roast will fit the cooker. Pressure cookers (at least mine) operate between atmospheric pressure (0.0 PSIG and 15.0 PSIG). PSIG stands for pounds per square inch gauge. Gauge means how much pressure above atmospheric pressure. The steam table tells us that water boils at 212 F at 0 PSIG. But with the lid on, the water in the pot boils until pressure reaches the set point. At 10 PSIG, the temperature is about 239F. At 15 PSIG, the temperature is about 250F. Either temperature is high enough to cut cooking time significantly compared with 212F. Notes: From: Vapor and Steam

Question: Why when a liquid reaches boiling point temperature stay constant? They say the added energy is latent heat but why temperature doesn't decrease when part of the liquid has evaporated and took energy with it to the air?
Answer: It has to do with the effects of energy on the liquid’s molecules. Let’s take water as an example. In liquid form, molecules have enough energy to be constantly moving around each other, kept in close proximity by weak attraction forces between molecules. They roll over each other and flow. As energy is increased, the molecules vibrate more and attraction forces are even weaker until the molecules break out of the liquid phase to form a gas or vapor. Here, they move in straight lines, separate, and are very weakly attracted to each other. As energy is applied to liquid water, its temperature increases (sensible heat) until molecules escape the liquid to form a gas. More energy serves to vaporize more molecules. At the same pressure, more heat cannot increase temperature, but can and does vaporize more molecules.

Question: What is the origin of eggplant Parmigiana? Are there health benefits to eating eggplant?
Answer: I’m convinced that nobody knows the true origin of eggplant Parmigiana. There are several stories but none with a direct link to Parmigiana Reggiano cheese though it is commonly used with this dish. But there is a link to the Parma Region, because it is a layered dish. Confused? Yeah, Buddy, me too. Eggplant did not make it to Italy until the 9th century, or the 15th depending on who you believe. It came from India by way of Arabians and is today linked with the Southern part of Italy, whereas Parma (where “The” cheese was) is over 600 miles away in Northern Italy. Sicily or Naples often get the nod for originating the dish. So why is Parmigiana in the dish’s name. Well, the stories mention one or two similar names and there’s always the region named Parma. 1) There’s a Sicilian word ‘parmiciana,’ for the overlapping wooden strips that form a shutter. Eggplant is also overlapped in a similar manner for eggplant Parmigiana. 2) When it first arrived in Southern Europe, eggplant was called ‘petronciana,’ a term of Persian origin. 3) Then, cheeses that were used were pecorino and in Naples, Mozzarella was added. The fact that today the dish is named after Parma, and, starting in the 15th and 16th centuries, “Parmigiana style” meant cooking with layered ingredients just like eggplant Parmigiana. All that points to Parma being the starting point. Now that we’ve cleared that up, we can discuss health and eggplants. Eggplants are low in carbohydrates, low-calorie, and a good fiber source. Then there’s the antioxidant content and rumors about heart disease risk protection due to anthocyanins and improved brain health by reducing inflammation. This seems contradictory to me, but the downsides of eggplants and other members of the nightshade family include alkaloids which are linked to inflammation. Lastly, eggplants have higher oxalates than most vegetables which could be a concern for your kidneys. I’m pretty confident that all these “facts” leave you just as confused as I am.

Question: What is the recipe for Chicken Cordon Bleu Stromboli?
Answer: There are many recipes for this online. They all boil down to rolling out a pizza dough or other bread dough into a thin dough in a rectanglular shape, lining the dough with slices of ham or Canadian bacon, overlapping some, and leaving an uncovered border around the edges. Then, Swiss cheese slices are layered over the ham and that is topped with seasoned, shredded, cooked chicken. A rotisserie chicken will do fine. Roll this up into a long, narrow tube, seal the seam and the ends and bake in a hot oven until the cheese is melted and the roll is nicely browned. I usually score the top to release steam. Lastly, cut into slices a few inches thick and serve with a dipping sauce. Ranch dressing, Dijon mustard, Alfredo sauce, mustard cream sauce or honey mustard sauce are all commonly used. I always make a pizza dough from scratch for Stromboli, but most recipes call for refrigerated bread, pizza or dinner roll doughs. Also some recipes online call for sliced deli chicken instead of shredded chicken. That’s okay, but my motto is, “Walk away from the deli chicken!” 🙂 But you do you. Question: What kind of feeling does the taste of bagels bring?
Answer: That’s impossible for me to give a simple answer, because good bagels come in a carnival of flavors; each bringing a slight change in feelings when enjoyed. It’s a little like walking into an interstate Buc-ee’s during vacation season. There’s the basic yeast bagel which is chewy and dense. All real bagels will have these characteristics. Eating a bagel involves a little work which is, to me, a satisfying feeling. Briefly boiling before baking cooks and gels the outside of the shaped bagel so its rise is restricted, making it dense and chewy … on purpose. The dough itself comes in various types from plain white dough, to rye, to multigrain, or a dough with nuts, herbs, fruits, or seeds. That way, you can feel nutty, poppy-ish, or raisiny, if you wish. Then the outside toppings, if any, can be poppy seeds, salt, onions, cheeses of several types, or cinnamon and sugar. Your mood can be sweet or savory. When sliced, you get to choose other toppings, or eat like a sandwich with great fillings. Cream cheese is a great topping and is called a “schmear.” That can feel cooling and very comforting and works with most types of bagels. Pardon me if you’ve heard me tell this story, but in high school, on a band trip, I walked into a deli by myself that advertised bagels. I had always heard of them, especially lox and bagels, on several TV shows. So, I sat at the counter with a several old men and proudly ordered, ‘Lox and bagels, please.” This brought a roar of laughter from the old men who asked, “Why in the world do you want that? I told them and they laughed again. I ate it, didn’t like it, but love them today. Brined salmon, capers, some onion, and cream cheese make a great bagel, but wait until after high school. What is Lox and Bagels? - The Mountain Kitchen A few bagels I made lo, those many years ago.

Question: How do I easily easily make homemade cheese and bacon scones?
Answer: I have an easy American biscuit recipe that you could try. The recipe below is very similar to a scone made without eggs. To use an egg, reduce the milk or buttermilk by 40 grams (~1 tablespoon). The recipe works for ham or breakfast sausage but for bacon, use thick bacon, chopped in 1/4″ to 1/2″ pieces and precook the bacon to remove most of the fat. Measure the cooked bacon by volume (5/8 to 2/3 cup), not by weight. Don't knead or work the dough too much, only mixing briefly, pressing, folding and pressing again is recommended. Also, when cutting, press the biscuit cutter all the way down and twist only when cutting is completed. Finally, shredded cheese tends to be absorbed while cubed cheese will melt and be visible in the dough and the exterior of the scone.

Question: Do those who are skilled at cooking at home (not professionals who cook en masse) prefer gas, electrical units, or induction method?
Answer: I’m with Diane Brand on this, gas is easier to control. By that, I mean, the gas knobs are graduated for help adjusting the heat, but those are not always linear. Notches around the low heat settings on my stovetop often have the same size of flame as the other. So on low heat settings, I watch the flame and make fine adjustments. At the high end of the scale, I find the graduated scale to be more reliable. Now, I can and do use electric ranges, but I have only the notches on the control knobs to go by. The control method is usually on-off or bang-bang control. The burner comes to high heat from being off and varies the time “on” versus “off” to control heat. That’s difficult for me to judge.

Question: Should you boil spareribs before baking or grilling?
Answer: Some do and I used to … many years ago. I’d suggest doing yourself a flavor by not boiling those pork ribs and diluting some of what this great cut has to offer. Instead, plan on cooking for several hours, prep the ribs, put a sweet, smoky rub on them, and cook on low heat (250F to 320F) in a smoker or with indirect heat on a grill using some hardwood or fruitwood smoke. Prepping spare ribs involves removing as much of the membrane as you reasonably can on the underside or backside of the ribs using a paper towel for gripping. A butter knife can also be useful to open up the membrane for grasping. Afterward, slather some mustard on the ribs before adding the rub. After cooking for two to three hours, depending on your temperature in the range, wrap the ribs in heavy duty foil and cook for an hour or so. Carefully drain any juices collected in the foil and remove the foil, and cook the ribs until the meat between the bones is 190F to 205F and the bones move when wiggled. If you add sauce or a glaze, do so for about 30 minutes at the end of the cook. Enjoy. It’s not hard.

Question: What are your memories of growing up in the Deep South?
Answer: I’m 75 but still growing up. Most of that time was as an adult with a family all living in Georgia. My childhood was spent in Texas, but I finished high school, college, and the university in Arkansas. After that was some time in Louisiana and back to Arkansas and finally, Georgia. My work after the University of Arkansas was for the same company at a few different plant locations. I retired after working 41 years in the chemical, aluminum and environmental fields again, for the same parent company. My memories include a great grandmother who raised my mother and her brothers by herself after Mom’s parents and paternal grandfather all passed away. My great grandmother was in her 60’s when she started raising these kids. My memories are of parents that loved us and worked very hard to provide all we needed but not all we wanted. They were excellent parents. During our time in Texas, we lived in an oil boom town which provided income for us. There are downsides to living in oil country, primarily with a smelly environment and pollution. That may have had something to do with the many years I worked cleaning up the environment and helping my company comply with environmental regulations. My time I lived in Louisiana (two short occasions) were important to me for the culture and foods in that area. Dad was in the country club restaurant business and later, a catering business in Louisiana for off-shore drilling rigs. Mom loved to cook and between those two influences, I developed a love for cooking and for Cajun/Creole foods. There were strong Christian influences in my family and that really helped me find a purpose and find peace. Finally, my daughter is dealing with MS and we are old, so we bought a large house for my wife and I and my daughter and her family to all share. I don’t know if that is a Southern thing, but it has really worked well for all of us. Did I mention growing up in an oil boom town?

Question: What are some intriguing examples of chemical reactions occurring in everyday life that we might not be aware of?
Answer: I can mention several reactions that I have experienced already this morning. We just checked out of a rental home and are currently driving back home. When a change occurs that is irreversible and something new is formed, that’s a chemical change. Early today, I cooked an omelette and egg whites changed from clear to white and the egg yolks changed from liquid to solid form. In the eggs and ham, proteins denatured and I concurrently browned some bread in the toaster which, I guess Is the malliard reaction at work. The dough was likely over proofed which just means the shaped loaf was allowed to rise for too long before baking and didn't have the strength to keep supporting the inflated loaf. I’ll make a suggestion to help prevent that in the future. Typically, dough is fermented after mixing and kneading in bulk, then divided into individual loaves, rolls, or buns and allowed to rise again before baking. The last rise is called proofing, but I don’t know why. In both periods of fermentation, bulk and proof, the dough should expand from 1 1/2 to 2 times its initial volume with some exceptions. The amount of rise is measurable. For bulk fermentation, a mixing bowl is a poor device for quantifying the volume increase; however, a transparent, straight sided container can be marked at the initial level and marked for what will be double that level. The container should be covered to prevent drying. For proofing, l take a 30 g (1 oz) sample of dough, form a ball and place it in an oiled, small juice glass or a graduated shot glass to measure the rise. The ball should be tamped flat and the shot glass marked for initial and doubled levels. Again, I cover the glass. I typically proof to 150% rise in volume before baking. The sample glass below appears larger than it is but it’s about a 4 oz glass and a 1 oz ± sample. The dough has risen or “proofed” 150% to 175% of its original volume here. If the dough in the glass and in the basket are at the same temperature and similar shape, they will rise at approximately the same rate.

Question: Why do recipes that want you to boil a liquid, say "bring to a boil"? Why not just "boil the liquid"?
Answer: Often, instructions are phrased that way to imply that a change is needed once the boil begins, or that cook time begins once the liquid is boiling. If I’m boiling an aqueous liquid (water or broth), I’ll start with high heat to minimize the cooking time and there is no ingredient that will suffer from the high heat. I’m expecting a change, like reducing the heat once a boil begins like to maintain a gentle simmer. For a lot of recipes (as with boiling eggs or for pasta), the instructions are to simmer or boil for X minutes. I start the timer once the boil begins and reduce the heat to a maintainable simmer or gentil boil, although with water and eggs or pasta, the rate of boil has a wide range with little difference in cook time. If I’m melting butter or sugar, I’ll use medium to low heat to prevent browning the butter while the water in the butter boils off or to prevent scorching the sugar after it melts.

Question: Why do some recipes have steps that require taking food out of the oven and letting it sit? 🏋🏻‍♀️
Answer: The step you are describing is usually called “resting” and is very common when cooking meats whether they are cooked in an oven, grill or smoker, or on a stovetop (hob). A related term is “carryover cooking,” a term which applies to the redistribution of heat in foods once removed from the cooking device. There are two purposes usually attributed to the resting of foods. The first applies to most solid foods (or semi-solid like casseroles) and the second to meats. The first, carryover cooking, is to allow the thickest portion or the portion farthest from the edges to finish rising in temperature after removing it from the cooking device. The second, resting meats, has to do with re-absorbing juices into the muscle-fibers of meats. Solid and semi-solid foods vary in temperature after cooking to some degree throughout the dish. The center of a casserole might be 160F while the edges are 175F or a pork chop may be 140F in the thickest part and 165F in the thinnest. When the casserole or pork chop are rested, the higher temperatures drop with heat losses to the room and to the lower temperature sections of the dish. After resting, the center and the edges of the casserole may be both be 160F and dropping. All portions, though will have reached the desired 165F, today’s “safe-to-eat” temperature. That’s carryover cooking. The image above depicts carryover cooking. The resting period for meats is called for to reduce the amount of meat juices released once the meat is cut. During a resting period, free juices are transformed into the meat for flavor and juiciness. This resting period is more important the hotter the meat is and the larger the cut is. Normally, it is 10 minutes or more between the time a smaller cut steak or pork chop is removed from the grill and is cut as it sits on someone’s plate. The cutting also begins on a cooler edge and not in the center of the steak or chop. The juices on smaller cuts have reabsorbed by the time we cut into the center. Larger cuts, like roasts, benefit from longer resting periods. The temperature in the center takes longer to rise while resting. In fact, BBQ gurus often remove large cuts, wrap them in foil and then towels and pack them in coolers for well over an hour. This produces exceptional tenderness and flavor in my experience and in the gurus’ experiences. In the photos below, a 10 minute rest stopped all loss of juices, but not shown is that a 5 minute rest stopped almost all the loss. I can seldom get a steak off the grill and onto a plate in front of a guest in 5 minutes, so resting a small cut of meat occurs naturally. A larger cut is a very different story. The Importance of Resting Meat | The Food Lab

Question: What are the key features to look for in the best offset smokers, and how do they enhance the flavor of smoked meats?

Price is related to your budget, usually to size, and depends on longevity as well. These often boil down to metal thickness and design. My first barrel grill/smoker was the style I had longed for since I was a kid in Texas, was inexpensive, and was rusted out in no time. Don’t be that guy or gal. Does the smoker function properly? Question: Why is it that recent water testing performed by the D.E.Q. in my area of the world found aluminum in all of its tributaries? Aluminum isn't bio-available in processed form, so where is it coming from?
Answer: Aluminum is the most abundant metal element in the earth’s crust. The largest source of aluminum in water is from leaching and runoff. Also, aluminum compounds (like alum) are used to settle suspended materials as part of many water treatment facilities. Aluminum is least soluble in pure water at a pH of 6 to 7 but the solubility rises rapidly as the pH decreases or increases. Acid rain is a factor in leaching aluminum from soils.
